questions.concept: A core multiplies the field by its relative permeability
questions.why: B = mu_r*mu_0*n*I = (250)(5.0e-3) = 1.3 T. Leaving it unchanged assumes the core is irrelevant, 3.1e-4 T is mu_r*mu_0 quoted as though it were a field, and dividing by 250 has the effect of a core exactly backwards.

questions.q: An electron has orbital angular momentum L = 1.05e-34 J*s. Taking g = 1, e = 1.60e-19 C and m = 9.11e-31 kg, the magnitude of its orbital magnetic moment is:
questions.concept: mu = g*e*L/(2m), the Bohr magneton for L = h-bar
questions.why: mu = (1.60e-19)(1.05e-34)/(2 x 9.11e-31) = 1.68e-53/1.82e-30 = 9.2e-24 J/T. Dividing by m rather than 2m doubles it, dividing by 4m halves it, and the negative version misreads a statement about direction as a negative magnitude.

questions.q: A circular coil of 25 turns and radius 5.0 cm carries 1.2 A in a uniform field of 0.50 T. Find (i) its magnetic dipole moment, (ii) the maximum torque it can experience, (iii) its potential energy when the normal makes 60 degrees with B, and (iv) the work done by the field as it turns from that orientation into alignment. Say what the sign of your answer to (iv) means.
questions.concept: mu = NIA for a circular coil, with torque, energy and the sign of the work
questions.why: (i) A = pi*r^2 = pi(0.050)^2 = 7.85e-3 m^2, so mu = (25)(1.2)(7.85e-3) = 0.236 A*m^2 - radius not diameter, and pi*r^2 not 2*pi*r. (ii) Maximum torque is at theta = 90 degrees, with the plane of the coil containing B: torque_max = mu*B = (0.236)(0.50) = 0.118 N*m. (iii) U(60) = -mu*B*cos(60) = -(0.118)(0.500) = -5.89e-2 J, negative because 60 degrees is nearer the aligned orientation than the anti-aligned one. (iv) U(0) = -0.118 J, so the work done by the field is -(U(0) - U(60)) = +5.89e-2 J. The positive sign means the field does the work: the dipole is falling into its energy minimum, and with nothing to damp it, it will overshoot and oscillate about theta = 0. An external agent guiding it slowly would do -0.0589 J, i.e. would have to absorb that energy.

questions.q: Two long parallel straight wires, 10 cm apart, each carry 5.0 A. Find the magnitude of the field each produces at the midpoint between them, then find the resultant field at that midpoint when (i) the currents are in the same direction and (ii) they are in opposite directions. Explain the difference in terms of the direction of each field, not merely the arithmetic.
questions.concept: Superposition of two wire fields, decided by direction
questions.why: Each wire is 0.050 m from the midpoint, so each contributes B = (2e-7)(5.0)/(0.050) = 2.0e-5 T. (i) Same direction, say both currents out of the page: each field circles its own wire anticlockwise, and because the midpoint lies on opposite sides of the two wires, the left wire's field points up the page there while the right wire's points down. They cancel exactly: the resultant is zero. (ii) Opposite directions: reversing one current reverses its whole circulation, so at the midpoint both fields point the same way and add to 4.0e-5 T, directed in the plane containing the wires and perpendicular to the line joining them. The lesson is that the result is the opposite of what naive addition suggests - parallel currents give zero field between them though they attract, antiparallel currents give the maximum field between them though they repel - and only the grip rule applied separately to each wire settles it.

questions.q: A solenoid 40 cm long is to produce an interior field of 12 mT with a current of 3.0 A and an air core. How many turns are needed? Then find the current that would give the same 12 mT if an iron core of relative permeability 200 were inserted and the winding left alone. Explain which quantity in B = mu*n*I each step is solving for, and why the answer to the first part does not depend on the solenoid's diameter.
questions.concept: Rearranging B = mu*n*I for the unknown quantity
questions.why: First part, solve for n and hence N: n = B/(mu_0*I) = 12e-3/((4*pi*1e-7)(3.0)) = 12e-3/3.77e-6 = 3.18e3 turns per metre, so N = n*L = (3183)(0.40) = about 1.3e3 turns (1273). Check: (4*pi*1e-7)(3183)(3.0) = 1.20e-2 T. Second part, solve for I with mu_r = 200: since B = mu_r*mu_0*n*I and both B and n are fixed, the current falls by the factor mu_r, giving I = 3.0/200 = 0.015 A (15 mA). The diameter does not enter because B = mu*n*I contains no radius: Ampere's law on a rectangular path of length l inside the solenoid, one long side on the axis and the other outside where B is about zero, gives B*l = mu*(n*l)*I, and the enclosed current depends only on l and n. Widening the coil enlarges the area each turn encloses but spreads the same current over a proportionally larger cross-section. A wider solenoid needs the same n and the same I, but more wire per turn and so more power for the same field.

questions.q: An electron with magnetic moment 9.3e-24 J/T sits in the 1.5 T field of an MRI magnet. Find its potential energy when aligned and when anti-aligned, and the energy needed to flip it. Convert that energy to electronvolts, and to the frequency of a photon that would supply it (h = 6.63e-34 J*s). Then explain why a real MRI scanner at 1.5 T operates at about 64 MHz rather than the frequency you just computed.
questions.concept: Dipole energies, the flip energy 2*mu*B, and interpreting the number
questions.why: Aligned U = -mu*B = -(9.3e-24)(1.5) = -1.4e-23 J; anti-aligned U = +1.4e-23 J. Flip energy = 2*mu*B = 2.79e-23 J. In electronvolts that is 2.79e-23/1.60e-19 = 1.7e-4 eV, some five thousand times smaller than a visible photon. The photon frequency is f = 2.79e-23/6.63e-34 = 4.2e10 Hz, about 42 GHz, in the microwave band. That number is for an electron moment, which is electron spin resonance, not MRI. Medical MRI flips the moments of hydrogen nuclei - protons - in the body's water, and a proton's moment is smaller than an electron's by roughly the mass ratio 1836, since the moment scales as e/2m: it is 1.41e-26 J/T. Repeating the calculation, 2*mu*B = 4.2e-26 J and f = 4.2e-26/6.63e-34 = 6.4e7 Hz = 64 MHz, in the radio band, exactly the operating frequency of a 1.5 T clinical scanner and the reason MRI is non-ionising. The physics is identical; only the mass in e/2m has changed, and that factor of about 2000 moves the answer from microwaves to radio.

checks.topic: Code work on abstraction, functions and modules: tracing a call through its parameters to the value it returns and to what appears on the screen, predicting the return of a void function or one whose return sits in the wrong place, spotting the scope, shadowing or pass-by-value fault in a fragment, reading escape sequences in a printf string, and choosing the correct decomposition and import form for a stated task

questions.q: What does this programme print? int bump(int x) { x = x + 3; return x * 2; } int main(void) { int a = 4; int b = bump(a); printf("%d %d\n", a, b); return 0; }
questions.concept: A parameter is a local copy; assigning to it cannot reach the caller's variable
questions.why: The call passes the VALUE of a, which is 4, into the parameter x. Inside bump, x becomes 7 and the function returns 7 * 2 = 14. Back in main, a was never touched - x is a separate variable that merely started with a copy of a's value - so a is still 4 and b is 14. Option b is the belief that x and a are the same variable under two names, the commonest error in the topic; if that were true, no function could safely use its parameters as working storage. Option c returns 4 * 2 and forgets that the body ran at all before the return. Option d makes both mistakes at once.

questions.q: 'void tax(double amt) { printf("%.2f\n", amt * 0.075); }', and a caller writes 'double t = tax(1000);'. What happens, and why?
options: t becomes 75.00, since that is the value the function worked out and put on the screen
t becomes 0, because a void function has nothing else to hand back and so hands back zero
t becomes 1000, because when a function returns no value the argument is passed straight back to the caller

The line is invalid: void is the return type of a function that returns no value at all, so there is nothing for t to receive - putting characters on the screen and handing a value back are different acts
questions.concept: void means no value returned; printing is not returning
questions.why: The return type void names a function that hands nothing back, so its call is a statement in its own right and cannot appear on the right of an equals sign. Option a is the trap the question exists for: the number 75.00 certainly appears, but printf sends characters to the screen and that is the end of them - nothing in the programme can pick them up again, and only return gives a value to the caller. Option b invents a default return value; 'returns nothing' and 'returns zero' are different states, and 'return 0;' would require the return type to be a number type in the first place. Option c invents a pass-back rule; arguments travel one way, into the parameters, and the parameters are copies.

questions.q: What does this print? int count = 0; void bump(void) { int count = 0; count = count + 1; } int main(void) { bump(); bump(); printf("%d\n", count); return 0; }
options: It does not compile, because the name count has already been used
questions.concept: Shadowing - a local with the same name as a global hides it, and assignments there never reach the global
questions.why: Inside bump, 'int count;' declares a NEW local variable, and every use of count in that body refers to it. Each call sets the local to 0, raises it to 1, and then the local is destroyed when the call ends. The global count is never mentioned inside bump at all, so it is still 0 when main prints it. Option a is the answer of someone who reads the two names as one variable and counts the two calls - it is what the programme would print if the line 'int count;' were deleted. Option b counts one call, which no reading supports. Option d treats a shadowed name as a redeclaration clash; it is legal precisely because the two names live in different scopes, which is what makes a function body private.

questions.q: You want exactly these two lines on the screen, the gaps being tab stops: line 1 'Name:' tab 'Ada', line 2 'Path:' tab 'C:\temp'. Which call produces them?
options: printf("Name:\tAda\nPath:\tC:\temp\n");
printf("Name:\tAda\nPath:\tC:\\temp\n");
printf("Name:\\tAda\\nPath:\\tC:\\temp\\n");
printf("Name:/tAda/nPath:/tC:/temp/n");
questions.concept: Reading escape sequences - every backslash inside a string starts one
questions.why: \t is a horizontal tab, \n a newline, and \\ is the escape whose meaning is a single backslash, so the second option gives Name:, tab, Ada, newline, Path:, tab, C:\temp, newline - exactly the target. Option a is the fault this question is about: in C:\temp the \t is ALSO read as an escape, so the second line comes out as 'Path:' tab 'C:' tab 'emp'; nothing in the source looks wrong, which is why the mistake survives being read back. Option c doubles every backslash, so nothing is an escape any more and the call prints the literal characters on one line. Option d uses forward slashes, which have no escape meaning at all in C - /t and /n print as themselves.

questions.q: A task: read three students' scores, print a letter grade for each, and print the average of the three. Which decomposition follows this week's material?
options: grade(score), which works out and prints one grade, and average3(a, b, c), which returns the mean; main reads the scores, calls grade three times and average3 once
gradeStudent1(s1), gradeStudent2(s2) and gradeStudent3(s3), one function per student so that each student's grading can later be changed on its own, plus main for the average
One function doEverything(a, b, c) holding the whole job, called once by main, so that all of the working is in a single place away from the entry point
No functions beyond main, since the task is small and every extra function is a further name that the reader of main has to go and look up
questions.concept: Decomposition - one function per specific task, written once however many times it is used
questions.why: The course's rule is that the division is up to the programmer but logically such that each function performs a specific task, and the stated benefit is that a function is implemented only once regardless of how many times it is used. Grading is one task needed three times, so it becomes one function called three times; averaging is a different task, so it is a different function. Option b is the exact inversion of the benefit: three functions with identical bodies is the duplication that functions exist to remove, and the excuse describes a requirement the task does not have. Option c puts the whole job in one function and renames the problem: doEverything performs no specific task, so nothing has been decomposed and nothing can be reused. Option d is the 'it's small now' answer that the course's opening argument answers directly - projects grow, more people join, and the point of functions is that the system remains stable as more are added.

questions.q: 'double bmi(double mass, double height) { return mass / (height * height); }'. A caller writes 'printf("%.4f\n", bmi(1.75, 70));', meaning a mass of 70 kg and a height of 1.75 m. What is printed?
options: 22.8571, since the compiler matches each argument to the parameter it was meant for by its type and its name
A compile error is reported, because 1.75 is not a plausible mass and the parameter is named mass
0.0004, because arguments bind to parameters strictly by position: mass takes 1.75 and height takes 70, and as both are double nothing warns you
0.0000, because dividing a small number by a much larger one gives a result that is truncated away before printing
questions.concept: Arguments bind to parameters by position
questions.why: bmi(1.75, 70) gives mass the value 1.75 and height the value 70, so the function computes 1.75 / (70 * 70) = 1.75 / 4900 = 0.000357..., printed to four places as 0.0004. The intended calculation was 70 / (1.75 * 1.75) = 70 / 3.0625 = 22.8571. Option a is the belief that the parameter's name or its meaning does the matching; names are for the reader, position is for the compiler. Option b expects the compiler to check plausibility; a compiler checks types, and both values are double, so the swap passes in complete silence - which is why this fault reaches the marked script. Option d invents integer truncation in a double expression; nothing here is an int, and 0.000357 is a perfectly representable value.

questions.q: What is printed? int twice(int n) { return n * 2; } int addOne(int n) { return n + 1; } int main(void) { printf("%d\n", twice(addOne(3))); return 0; }
questions.concept: A nested call is evaluated inside-out; its return value becomes the argument to the outer call
questions.why: addOne(3) runs first and returns 4; that 4 is then the argument passed to twice, which returns 8, and 8 is the argument printf displays. Option b, 7, is addOne(twice(3)) - the two functions applied in the wrong order, which is what you get by reading the line left to right as though the outer name acted first. Option a, 6, drops addOne entirely and computes twice(3). Option d, 9, adds one after doubling, the same order error worked from the other end. Only one of the four is what the brackets say, and the brackets are the whole content of the question.

questions.q: What does sumTo(4) return? int sumTo(int n) { int s = 0; int i = 1; while (i <= n) { s = s + i; i = i + 1; return s; } return 0; }
options: 10, since the loop runs while i <= 4 and s accumulates 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 before the finished total is handed back
1, because return does not merely end the current pass of the loop - it ends the whole function at once, on the first pass, when s is still 1
4, because a return placed inside a loop hands back the number of passes the loop completed
0, because a return inside a loop body is skipped and the function falls through to the 'return 0;' at the bottom
questions.concept: return ends the function immediately, not just the loop pass
questions.why: The loop body runs once: s becomes 0 + 1 = 1, i becomes 2, and then 'return s;' executes - which hands 1 back and terminates sumTo on the spot. The condition i <= n is never tested a second time and the 'return 0;' at the bottom is never reached. Option a is what the function was meant to do and what it would do if the 'return s;' were moved below the closing brace of the loop; it is the answer of anyone who reads return as 'end this pass'. Option c invents a meaning for return inside a loop; return hands back the value of the expression written after it, and that expression is s. Option d is the belief that the last return in a function is the one that counts; execution reaches at most one return, and it is whichever one it meets first.

questions.q: Trace this programme and state exactly what it prints, then explain why the global total holds the value it does, naming the mechanism; say which one line you would delete to make add update the global instead, and why that would be a bad trade. Programme: 'int total = 0;' at file scope; 'int add(int a, int b) { int total; total = a + b; return total; }'; 'void report(int v) { printf("v = %d, total = %d\n", v, total); }'; 'int main(void) { int x = 3, y = 5; int r = add(x, y); total = total + 1; report(r); return 0; }'.
questions.concept: Tracing a programme with a shadowed global; what a function's interface does and does not include
questions.why: It prints 'v = 8, total = 1'. Trace: main sets x = 3, y = 5 and calls add(3, 5). Inside add the parameters a and b receive 3 and 5, and the line 'int total;' declares a LOCAL variable of that name, which shadows the global for the whole of add's body. 'total = a + b;' therefore writes 8 into the local, and 'return total;' hands that 8 back, so r is 8. When add returns, its local total ceases to exist and the global - never mentioned inside add - is still 0. main then executes 'total = total + 1;', and here there is no local of that name in scope, so this IS the global: it becomes 1. report(8) receives 8 into its parameter v and prints the global total, which it can see because a global is visible to every function in the file. The mechanism is shadowing, and the value 8 got out of add by the only route it had - the return value. The one-line deletion: remove 'int total;' from add; then the name inside add resolves to the global and the programme would print 'v = 8, total = 9'. Why that is a bad trade: add's header, 'int add(int a, int b)', states its input format and its output format, and after the deletion it no longer tells the truth, because the function would also silently write to something the caller never passed and never received. Every caller then has to know its internals - the thing functional abstraction exists to prevent - and the benefit that the implementation can be changed without breaking other parts of the code is lost, because body and callers now share state. Concretely: main would have to know whether to increment total before or after calling add, and any second function that also wrote to total would make add's effect depend on the order in which the two were called. The local costs one line and buys a function whose header is a complete description of it.

questions.q: This is meant to exchange two values, and does not. State what it prints, explain exactly what went wrong in terms of what a parameter is, and give two different repairs - one that keeps the values in the caller and one that changes what is passed - saying what each repair costs. Code: 'void swap(int a, int b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }' and 'int main(void) { int p = 2, q = 9; swap(p, q); printf("%d %d\n", p, q); return 0; }'.
questions.concept: Pass-by-value - a parameter receives a copy, so a function cannot alter the caller's variables through one
questions.why: It prints '2 9', unchanged. What went wrong: the course says a parameter is like a placeholder, and that when a function is invoked a value is passed to the parameter. A VALUE is passed, not the variable itself: a and b are two fresh local variables of swap that begin life holding copies of 2 and 9. The body swaps those copies perfectly - after the three lines a is 9 and b is 2 - and then swap returns, its locals are destroyed, and p and q, which were never touched, still hold 2 and 9. The function is not wrong about swapping; it is swapping the wrong two variables, and it has no way to reach the right ones because nothing about p and q was ever passed to it. Repair 1, keep the values in the caller: do the exchange where the variables live, 'int t = p; p = q; q = t;' in main. Cost: the exchange is no longer a named, reusable piece of the programme - if it is needed in five places it is written five times, exactly the duplication functions exist to prevent - and a function can return only one value, so a single swap returning both is not available at this level. Repair 2, change what is passed: pass the addresses of the caller's variables, 'void swap(int *a, int *b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; }', called as 'swap(&p, &q);', which then prints '9 2'. Cost: the interface is harder - the caller must write & and the body must write * - and the header now advertises that the function reaches into the caller's variables, a real loss of abstraction, which is exactly why it must be visible in the header rather than hidden. The general lesson: if a function must change something the caller holds, that has to be part of its declared interface, either as a returned value or as something explicitly passed; it can never happen by accident through an ordinary parameter.

questions.q: A programme must read three test scores, print A for a score of 70 or more, Pass for 50 or more, Fail otherwise, then print the average of the three. The first draft writes the whole if/else-if/else chain out three times inside main and computes the average with (a + b + c) / 3. Rewrite it as a decomposition into functions: give each function's header and body, say for one call which value is the argument and which name is the parameter, state what the programme prints for the scores 82, 64 and 41, and explain the one arithmetic fault in (a + b + c) / 3.
questions.concept: Extracting a repeated block into a function, and integer division
questions.why:
Two specific tasks appear in the statement - deciding and printing one grade, and averaging three numbers - so there are two functions. 'void printGrade(int score) { if (score >= 70) printf("A
"); else if (score >= 50) printf("Pass
"); else printf("Fail
"); }' and 'double average3(int a, int b, int c) { return (a + b + c) / 3.0; }', with main holding 'int s1 = 82, s2 = 64, s3 = 41;', three calls to printGrade and one to average3, printed with %.2f. The grading chain is now written once and used three times, which is the course's stated benefit; printGrade is void because its job is to put characters on the screen, while average3 has a return type because its job is to hand a number back for main to print. Parameter and argument at one call: in printGrade(s1) the PARAMETER is score - the placeholder written once in the header - and the ARGUMENT is the value of s1, namely 82, supplied at this particular call; the next call supplies 64 to the same parameter. What it prints: A, then Pass, then Fail, then 62.33 - because 82 >= 70 gives A, 64 fails 70 but meets 50 giving Pass, 41 fails both giving Fail, and the sum 82 + 64 + 41 = 187 divided by 3 is 62.333..., shown to two places as 62.33. The arithmetic fault in (a + b + c) / 3: all three scores are int and 3 is an int, so this is INTEGER division - the fractional part is discarded rather than rounded, and 187 / 3 evaluates to 62, not 62.33. Storing the result in a double afterwards does not help, because the damage is done before the assignment; the fix is to make one operand a real number, / 3.0, so the division is done in floating point. The error is invisible whenever the total happens to divide exactly, which is why it survives testing on tidy sample data.

questions.q: A module file 'special_functions' contains the functions max and min. Write both import forms, and beside each write the call that finds the larger of 4 and 7. Then say for each form which names have become usable in your code and which have not. Finally, explain what is wrong with the two lines 'import special_functions' followed by 'm = max(4, 7)', and give the two different one-line fixes.
questions.concept: The two import forms, and what each makes usable
questions.why: The two forms with the matching call: 'import special_functions' then 'm = special_functions.max(4, 7)'; or 'from special_functions import max' then 'm = max(4, 7)'. What each makes usable: after 'import special_functions', the name special_functions is usable and through it every function and class in the module - special_functions.max, special_functions.min - while the bare names max and min are NOT usable, since nothing has been added to your code's own names. After 'from special_functions import max', the name max is usable directly; what is NOT usable is min, because you explicitly specified the exact function you want and, as the course puts it, you can only use the max function - and the name special_functions is not made available either, so special_functions.min(4, 7) fails as well. What is wrong with the fragment: it imports the module and then calls max as though the second form had been used. The module has been made available under its own name, but no name called max has been introduced into this code, so max(4, 7) does not name the module's function. The two one-line fixes work in opposite places: keep the import and qualify the call, 'm = special_functions.max(4, 7)'; or keep the call and change the import, 'from special_functions import max'. The choice is the ordinary trade this week is about - qualifying the call keeps it obvious which module a function came from at the cost of a longer line every time, while importing the name directly keeps calls short at the cost of hiding where max came from and of introducing a name that may collide with one of your own. Either way, what you know about max is only its name and the format of its input and output, which is why the same mechanism appears in C as #include of a header file.

recapCandidates.topic: Integration by parts: that (integral of u dv) = uv - (integral of v du) trades one integral for another rather than evaluating it, so the choice of u and dv is what decides whether the trade is progress, and an integral that reappears is the method working rather than failing
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students meet parts as a formula to be filled in, and the formula can be filled in for any product whatsoever - which is exactly the problem. Because both assignments of u and dv produce a valid line of algebra, the belief forms that the choice is cosmetic: pick either, and the answer will come out with more or fewer lines. What actually happens is that the wrong choice trades the integral for a strictly harder one - in (integral of x^3 ln x dx), taking u = x^3 gives v = (integral of ln x dx), which is itself a parts problem, and in (integral of x cos x dx), taking u = cos x raises the power of x from 1 to 2, so every further application makes it worse. The second half of the misunderstanding is what counts as an answer. Parts hands back another integral sign, and a student who believes a technique must deliver a closed form reads that as failure, gives up, or quietly drops the (integral of v du) term and reports uv alone. That belief is fatal in the cycling integrals (integral of e^x sin x dx) and (integral of e^x cos x dx), where the original integral I genuinely reappears and the answer comes from treating the equation I = e^x sin x - e^x cos x - I as an equation and solving 2I = ..., a step that looks like cheating to someone who thinks integration only ever moves forwards. Both errors survive self-checking because the student never differentiates the result: uv alone differentiates to u dv + v du, which contains the integrand as one of its two terms, so a quick glance appears to confirm it, and a wrong u/dv choice usually ends not in a wrong answer but in an abandoned page, which reads as 'this one was too hard' rather than 'I chose badly'. LIATE is then memorised as a magic ordering rather than as a summary of the two real conditions - dv must be something you can integrate, and u should be something that collapses when differentiated.
whyQuestions: Why does integration have no product rule, when differentiation has one?
Why does the formula (integral of u dv) = uv - (integral of v du) count as progress at all, given that the right-hand side still contains an integral?
Why, in (integral of x^3 ln x dx), does taking u = ln x work while taking u = x^3 does not - what exactly goes wrong in the second case?
Why does (integral of e^x sin x dx) come back to itself after two applications, and why is that a solvable situation rather than a dead end?
Why must the second application of parts in a cycling integral keep the exponential as dv, and what precisely happens to the equation if you swap the roles instead?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
That parts is the product rule d(uv) = u dv + v du integrated and rearranged, so it exchanges (integral of u dv) for a boundary term uv plus a different integral (integral of v du), and promises nothing about that new integral being easier.
That the choice of u and dv is governed by two conditions, not by a mnemonic: dv must be integrable to get v at all, and u should simplify when differentiated - which is why the algebraic factor is u against a trigonometric or exponential dv (the power drops by one each time and the process terminates), while a logarithm is u because it has no antiderivative to serve as dv.
That an integral reappearing is not failure: in the cycling case the identity is treated as an algebraic equation in I and solved, and the whole result is then checked by differentiating it back to the integrand.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
Evaluate I = (integral of e^x cos x dx).

Step 1 - first application. Take u = cos x, dv = e^x dx, so du = -sin x dx and v = e^x.
  I = e^x cos x - (integral of e^x (-sin x) dx) = e^x cos x + (integral of e^x sin x dx).
The new integral is no simpler than the old one - but it is no worse either, and that is the signal to apply parts a second time rather than to give up.

Step 2 - second application, keeping e^x as dv again. Let J = (integral of e^x sin x dx), and take u = sin x, dv = e^x dx, so du = cos x dx and v = e^x.
  J = e^x sin x - (integral of e^x cos x dx) = e^x sin x - I.

Step 3 - solve for I. Substituting J back into Step 1:
  I = e^x cos x + e^x sin x - I
  2I = e^x (sin x + cos x)
  I = e^x (sin x + cos x)/2 + C.

Step 4 - check by differentiating. d/dx [e^x (sin x + cos x)/2] = e^x (sin x + cos x)/2 + e^x (cos x - sin x)/2 = e^x (2 cos x)/2 = e^x cos x. Correct.

What the wrong choice does. Suppose that at Step 2 you swap the roles and take u = e^x, dv = sin x dx, so v = -cos x:
  J = -e^x cos x + (integral of e^x cos x dx) = -e^x cos x + I.
Substituting into Step 1 gives I = e^x cos x - e^x cos x + I, that is I = I - a true statement carrying no information. The second application must undo nothing: whichever factor was dv the first time must be dv again, or the two steps cancel.

recapCandidates.topic: What actually crosses the boundary of a function call - a parameter receives a copy, and returning a value is not the same as printing one
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students learn the words of this week easily - a function is a group of statements that perform a task, a parameter is like a placeholder, the return type is the data type of the value the function returns - and can recite all of it while holding a mental picture that is wrong in one specific way: they imagine that naming a variable in a call somehow gives the function that variable. On that picture, 'passing n' means the function now has n, so anything it does to it happens to n; and 'the function produced the number' means the number is now available, whether it came out through a return or through printf. Both halves of the picture are false, and each one produces a family of bugs that look like different topics until you see they are the same. From the first half come the mutated-parameter faults: a void function that 'updates' a price and changes nothing, a swap that swaps two copies, a loop counter that a helper function was supposed to advance and did not. From the second half come the missing-return faults: a function with a non-void return type whose body only prints, a void function assigned to a variable, a caller that calls a function and then wonders where the answer went. The reason the wrong belief survives self-checking is that the evidence usually agrees with it. The number does appear on the screen, because printf ran; the calculation inside the function is right, because the student traced it and it was; the programme compiles, because C is perfectly happy to let you assign to a parameter and, in a beginner's compiler settings, will not stop you writing a function that falls off the end without returning. The single test that would expose the belief - print the caller's variable after the call, not the function's - is the one thing the student does not do, because on their picture there is nothing to check. Two further confusions sit on top. 'Returns nothing' gets collapsed into 'returns zero', so void looks like a value rather than the absence of one. And scope gets read as a nuisance instead of as the mechanism doing the work: a local that shadows a global, or a parameter that hides one, is seen as a naming accident rather than as the language enforcing that a function body is private - which is why the reflex fix, making the variable global so everyone can reach it, feels like a simplification while actually destroying the property that made functions worth having.
whyQuestions: Why does a function need a parameter at all, when the value it wants is already sitting in a variable in main?
Why does assigning a new value to a parameter inside a function leave the caller's variable completely unchanged?
Why is printing a value not the same as returning it, when in both cases the number ends up on the screen?
Why does a local variable that shares its name with a global leave the global untouched - and why is that the right rule rather than a trap for the unwary?

Why does moving a variable out to global scope, so that functions need not pass it around, destroy the very guarantee - that an implementation can be changed without breaking other parts of the code - that abstraction was supposed to deliver?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Names what physically crosses the boundary at a call: the ARGUMENT's value is copied into the PARAMETER, which is a new local variable belonging to that call and destroyed when it ends, so the caller's variable is not reachable from inside and assigning to a parameter changes only the copy.
Names the only two ways anything gets back out, and keeps them apart: the RETURN VALUE, which the caller can store, test and pass on, and which requires a non-void return type; and side effects such as printf, which put characters on the screen where no part of the programme can retrieve them - so 'it printed 75' and 'it returned 75' are different facts, and void means there is no value at all to assign, not that the value is zero.
Ties both to the week's abstraction: a function's header - name, parameters, return type - is exactly the course's 'name, format of the input, format of the output', so anything that crosses the boundary without appearing in the header (a global read or written inside the body) is a hidden dependency that makes the header a lie and forfeits the benefit that the body can be rewritten without breaking callers.
